model.name: H.R. 7934 (119th)
model.title: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026

summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House):

blocks.text: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
This bill requires federal agencies to publish a searchable, online database of information about certain settlement agreements entered into by the agency. The database must include
a copy of each settlement agreement,
whether the agreement resolves a civil or criminal claim (or both),
the date the agreement was executed,
any alleged statutory violations,
the amount of attorneys fees provided by or to the United States,
any payment made to or by the federal government,
the projected duration of the agreement, and
any unit of government that is identified by the terms of the agreement.
In general, the bill applies to settlement agreements that
require at least $10 million in payments by a settling party;
involve the appointment of a special master or monitor;
involve a party that is a state, county, or local government; or
meet other criteria as determined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).

The bill excludes several types of settlement agreements from the database, including agreements related to a federal employee personnel action, a non-prosecution agreement or plea bargain, or the Internal Revenue Code.
To extent practicable, the bill also applies retroactively to covered settlement agreements that were entered into on or after January 1, 2015, and remain in effect on or after the date of enactment.
The OMB must issue guidance to implement the bill.

The Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026 would require federal agencies to publish a searchable online database with details about certain settlements they enter into. For each covered settlement, the database must include a copy of the agreement, whether it resolves a civil claim, a criminal claim, or both, the date it was signed, any laws the other side is alleged to have broken, the amount of attorneys' fees paid by or to the United States, any payments made to or by the federal government, how long the agreement is expected to last, and any government unit named in the agreement.

The rules would generally cover settlements that require at least $10 million in payments from a party, that involve appointing a special master or monitor, or that involve a state, county, or local government. The Office of Management and Budget could also add other qualifying criteria.

Several kinds of settlements would be left out of the database. These include agreements about personnel actions involving federal employees, non-prosecution agreements and plea bargains, and agreements under the Internal Revenue Code.
The bill would also reach back in time, to the extent practical. It would cover qualifying settlements made on or after January 1, 2015, that are still in effect when the law takes effect.
Finally, the Office of Management and Budget would be required to issue guidance to carry out the law.
